lead: Three sheet processes shape metal without cutting it. Stretch forming grips the sheet at its edges and pulls it over a form block; the sheet is stretched by tension, so it takes the block's shape and springs back very little. Embossing and coining press the sheet between closed dies so the die surface is copied onto the metal. Embossing makes shallow raised patterns. Coining squeezes the metal hard enough to change its thickness. You meet these in aircraft skins, car panels, nameplates and the coins in your pocket.
prereq: You need: strain, necking and forming limits from 3.1, and springback from 3.3.

sections.h3: Stretch forming: tension over a form block

blocks.text: A stretch forming press holds the blank by its two long edges in serrated jaws called grips. A rigid form block, shaped like the inside of the finished part, sits between the grips. The block rises into the sheet, or the grips move apart, and the sheet is pulled over the block. The sheet stays under tensile stress while it touches the block, so it wraps the block tightly instead of merely bending over it.

blocks.where: e is the engineering strain (no unit); ε is the true strain (no unit); L_f is the final gripped length in mm; L_0 is the original gripped length in mm; ln is the natural logarithm. Both strains are positive in tension.

blocks.text: Springback is the elastic recovery after the load is removed. In stretch forming the sheet carries membrane tension, and the bending stress through the thickness is small beside it. Only the elastic part comes back, roughly the yield strain, near 0.2% for aluminium, so the part stays close to the block. Plain bending springs back far more (see 3.3).

items: Clamp the blank edges in the serrated grips, leaving a scrap margin.
Bring the form block up until it touches the middle of the sheet.
Pull the grips apart until the sheet wraps the whole block surface.
Hold for a moment, release the load, and trim off the gripped margin.

blocks.text: Parts made this way: aircraft fuselage and wing skins, wing leading edges, large car body panels, sink bowls and curtain-wall panels. Aluminium alloys, titanium and austenitic stainless steel are chosen because they stretch far before necking (see 3.1). Only shallow, gently contoured shapes pay off; single curvature is easiest, compound curvature is possible, and deep or sharply cornered shapes tear. The margin under the teeth is deformed and becomes scrap.

sections.h3: Embossing and coining: pressing detail into the sheet

blocks.text: Embossing uses a matched pair of dies: one carries the pattern raised, the other carries the same pattern sunk. The sheet is pressed between them, and the pattern stands out on one face and sinks in on the other. The metal flows mainly in its own plane, so the thickness change is small and the pattern depth is usually less than the sheet thickness. Foil, nameplates, instrument dials, appliance panels and the stiffening ribs on car panels are embossed.

Coining also uses closed dies, but the cavity is sealed by a rim or collar, so the metal has nowhere to escape. The press squeezes at very high pressure, the metal flows in all directions, and the thickness changes on purpose. A coin is the standard example: the blank is thicker than the finished coin at its flat field, and the die faces and the collar close on it, so one or two blows force the surplus metal into the rim and the relief on both faces at once. Coining also makes medals, jewellery, dental caps and small precision parts. The flow is severe, so blanks are often annealed between blows and the dies are hard tool steel or carbide.
All three shape the sheet by pressure, not by cutting, and none of them needs the punch-and-die clearance of blanking. What separates them is the state of stress in the metal.

items: Stretch forming: tension across the whole sheet, one form block, large gentle parts, low springback.
Embossing: compression between matched dies, shallow pattern, thickness nearly constant.
Coining: compression with the cavity closed, deep relief, thickness changes deliberately.

blocks.text: Faults to watch. In stretch forming, tearing starts at the grips or at a sharp corner of the block, and coarse grains give an orange-peel surface. In embossing, too much depth tears the thin wall of the pattern. In coining, an oversized blank folds into laps because the surplus metal has nowhere to go.

figure.caption: Grips pull the clamped sheet so it wraps the form block; releasing gives the stretched skin. Notice that the pull is what holds the sheet on the block and keeps springback low.

examples.question: A 1.2 mm thick aluminium sheet is stretch formed. The length between the grips is 800 mm before the pull and 860 mm after it. (a) Find the engineering strain. (b) Find the true strain. (c) Estimate the final thickness, assuming the width does not change. (d) Say why the two strains differ.
steps: Known values: original gripped length L_0 = 800 mm, final gripped length L_f = 860 mm, original thickness t_0 = 1.2 mm.
Constant volume with no width change gives t_f = t_0 / (L_f / L_0) = 1.2 / 1.075 = 1.116 mm, so the sheet thins by 1.2 − 1.116 = 0.084 mm.

Difference between the strains = 0.075 − 0.0723 = 0.0027. It is small because the stretch is small; at 50% stretch the gap becomes large, and true strain is the correct measure there because it adds up the strain of each small increment.
examples.answer: e = 0.075 (7.5%), ε = 0.0723, and the sheet thins from 1.2 mm to about 1.116 mm.
examples.check:
import math
L0 = 800.0
Lf = 860.0
t0 = 1.2
e = (Lf - L0) / L0
eps = math.log(Lf / L0)
tf = t0 / (Lf / L0)
print(round(e, 3))
print(round(eps, 4))
print(round(tf, 3))

traps: Saying embossing and coining both keep the thickness constant. Coining changes thickness on purpose; embossing changes it very little.
Using engineering strain where true strain belongs. At 7.5% stretch the gap is small (0.075 against 0.0723), but at large stretch true strain is the one that adds up.
Drawing a matching die cavity for stretch forming. There is only a form block; the sheet is pulled over one surface, not squeezed between two.
Writing ε = ln(L_0 / L_f). The ratio is final over original, so ε comes out positive in tension.
Believing stretch forming removes springback completely. It only reduces it; a small elastic recovery always remains.

quiz.q: Define engineering strain and true strain for a stretched sheet.
quiz.a: Engineering strain e = (L_f − L_0)/L_0, based on the original length. True strain ε = ln(L_f/L_0), which adds the strain of each small increment. L_f is the final length and L_0 the original length, both in mm.

quiz.q: Why is springback smaller in stretch forming than in simple bending?
quiz.a: In bending only a thin outer layer yields while the core stays elastic, so the recovery is a large share of the bend. In stretch forming the whole section is above yield in membrane tension, with little bending stress through the thickness, so the recovered elastic strain is only about the yield strain.

quiz.q: A sheet is stretched from 500 mm to 540 mm between grips. Find the engineering strain and the true strain.
A stretch-formed part must reach a true strain of 0.05. By what percentage does its length increase?
quiz.a: ε = ln(L_f/L_0) = 0.05, so L_f/L_0 = e^0.05 = 1.0513. The length increases by 5.13%.

quiz.q: Give two differences between embossing and coining.
quiz.a: Embossing uses matched dies and makes shallow detail with almost no thickness change; coining uses a closed die with a rim, very high pressure, and changes thickness. In embossing the pattern is raised on one face and sunk on the other; coining fills fine relief through the full thickness.

quiz.q: A coining die is built without a rim or collar. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: The metal escapes sideways instead of being forced into the detail, so the pressure stays low, the relief is not filled, and the blank spreads and thickens unevenly. The rim is what seals the cavity and keeps the stress high.

quiz.q: Why are the grips serrated, and why is the gripped margin scrapped?
quiz.a: Serrations stop the sheet slipping so the full pull reaches the sheet instead of the jaws. The teeth leave notches and the metal under the grips is deformed, so a margin is left outside the part and trimmed off.

quiz.q: Name two products made by coining and two made by embossing.
quiz.a: Coining: coins and medals. Embossing: nameplates and the ribbed panels on appliances.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, stretch forming is often helped or replaced by hydroforming, where oil at high pressure pushes the sheet onto a one-sided tool; tube hydroforming makes bicycle frame parts and car exhaust sections. High-energy-rate forming uses an explosive charge or a magnetic pulse instead of a slow press. Springback compensation by die correction and by active blank-holder control is an active research area. Search for stretch forming of aircraft skins, coin minting process, and sheet hydroforming.
